items.title: Why the flag key is part of the hash input
items.body:
bucket() hashes the string `${flagKey}:${salt}:${distinctId}`. Because the flag key is in the input, flag A and flag B give a user two unrelated bucket values. Without it, every experiment would split users the same way: the people in "test" for one experiment would be in "test" for all of them, and their effects would be confounded. The property tests (chi-square and Pearson) exist to catch exactly that.

- "Move a user by editing the key" is a side effect of a new key (a new experiment), not the reason it is hashed.
- "Only a cache key" is wrong: the key is literally in the hashed string.
- "To make the hash slower" is wrong: FNV-1a is chosen for being cheap.

excerpts.quote: return hash32(`${flagKey}:${salt}:${distinctId}`) / 0x100000000;
the flagKey is IN the hash input, so experiments don't share a split.

items.title: Concept: assigning variants with a hash instead of a table
items.body:
Pulse assigns users to flag variants with a hash instead of an assignment table. Every evaluator (the server, the SDK and backfill jobs) calls `bucket(...)` in `packages/shared/src/bucketing.ts`, which hashes a string with FNV-1a, finishes it with murmur3's fmix32 mixer and divides by 2^32 to land in [0, 1). Same inputs give the same number on every machine, with no database and no communication.

While reading, work out for yourself exactly what goes into the hashed string and why each part is there. Then read `evaluateFlag` in `packages/flags/src/evaluate.ts` top to bottom and list its checks in the order they run, with the reason string each early return gives. Note how many times it calls `bucket` and with which salts. Finally, take one user and a flag, change only the rollout percentage, and decide from the code whether that user's numbers change.

S14 closes the analytics loop: the product ships feature flags, and measures their effect with A/B experiments. Two design questions decide everything downstream: **how is a user assigned to a variant**, and **how do we decide an experiment worked**.

items.title: Start here: Pulse writes its analytics semantics down as contracts
items.body:
Pulse is a product-analytics platform: an SDK sends events, an ingest service accepts them, and query code turns them into funnels, experiments and sampled charts. This quest is about the places where a number could quietly mean two different things, and how Pulse pins each one down in writing.

Read in this order. `docs/funnel-semantics.md` is the funnel contract for analysts; keep `packages/insights/src/funnel.ts` open beside it. Then ADR-0011 and `docs/experiments/peeking.md` cover how users are assigned to variants and how an experiment is judged; the code is `packages/shared/src/bucketing.ts`, `packages/flags/src/evaluate.ts` and `packages/flags/src/results.ts`. Finish with three short ADRs: 0003 (API keys), 0009 (the live tail) and 0010 (sampling).

Most questions give you a small timeline or a setting and ask what the code does. Trace the code line by line rather than guessing from the doc wording.

excerpts.quote: A funnel query is a **contract**: "conversion" has to mean exactly one thing, or two people run the same funnel

readMore.why: The single-pass funnel state machine; about 60 lines carry every funnel rule.

items.title: A breakdown labels each person once
items.body:
`computeFunnelBreakdown` first scans the events and, for each person, stores a label from the FIRST step-1 event it meets (`if (!labelOf.has(person))`). Then it puts every event of that person into that one group and runs a normal funnel per group. A person whose first view was on Firefox is in the Firefox group, even if all later events say Chrome.

One precision: "first" here means first in the order the events arrive in the input array. This loop does not sort; the time sort happens only inside `computeFunnel` (funnel.ts:50). With time-ordered input the two agree.

- "Both groups" would double-count people; the label map holds one label per person.
- "The majority browser" is not computed anywhere.
- "(none)" is only used when the property is missing or null on that first event.

excerpts.quote: if (!labelOf.has(person)) {

items.title: Concept: a funnel is a tiny state machine per person
items.body:
`computeFunnel` turns a list of events into step counts. It groups events by person and then walks each person's events with a couple of local variables: `level` (how many steps are done) and `anchor` (a timestamp the window is measured from).

Treat it as a tiny state machine and trace it by hand. Write down, for each event, which branch of the loop it takes. Pin down four things from the code rather than from the contract page: the order the events are walked in, the exact moment `anchor` is assigned (and whether it can ever be reassigned), what the window check compares the event time against and with which operator, and what happens to an event that matches a step out of order.

Then read the last lines of the loop to see how a person's final `level` turns into counts per step. `computeFunnelBreakdown` sits next to it: note how it decides which group a person belongs to, and whether it sorts first.

items.title: Order matters: a step before its predecessor is ignored
items.body:
Walk the events in time order. The day-0 signup comes first, while `level` is 0, and the only thing that can match at level 0 is step 1. So the signup is skipped. The day-1 view then sets the anchor and level 1. No later signup exists, so the person ends at level 1 and counts at step 1 only.

- "Order is ignored inside the window" contradicts rule 3: steps must occur in sequence.
- "The person is discarded" is wrong: reaching step 1 is enough to be counted as an entrant.
- "Counts at step 2" would need the signup to come AFTER the anchor.

items.title: Pooled for the test, separate variances for the interval
items.body:
The z-test asks "could these two rates be equal?", so under that null hypothesis it pools them: `pooled = (c1 + c2) / (n1 + n2)` and the standard error uses that one rate. The confidence interval describes the difference we actually estimated, so it uses each arm's own variance: `seUnpooled` adds `rate * (1 - rate) / exposed` per arm.

- "Pooled for both" is wrong for the interval; the code comment says the CI deliberately uses the unpooled SE.
- "Unpooled for both" is wrong for the z-test.
- "Separate variances in the test, shared rate for the interval" is the exact reverse of the code.

excerpts.quote: const pooled = (c1 + c2) / (n1 + n2);

items.title: Peeking turns a 5% test into a 26% one
items.body:
Both arms of an A/A test share the same 10% conversion rate, so every "significant" result is false by construction. Checking after every 100 samples and stopping at the first p < 0.05 gives about 26% false positives in the simulation; one look at the planned sample size gives about 4.7%.

Why: a p-value is calibrated for ONE look. Each extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line, and the peeker stops exactly at that random high point.

- "About 5%" is the fixed-horizon rate, not the peeking rate.
- "About 50%" overstates the table.
- "Zero" confuses "the true lift is zero" with "no test can come out significant".

excerpts.quote: | **Peeking** | check p after every 100 samples, stop the first time p < 0.05 | **~26%** |
A p-value is calibrated for **one** look.

items.title: evaluateFlag returns at the first check that fails
items.body:
Read `evaluateFlag` top to bottom. It returns "disabled" if the flag is off. Next, if the flag has targeting filters and the user's properties do not match them all, it returns the control variant with reason "not_targeted". Only a targeted user reaches the rollout draw and can get "out_of_rollout". A user who fails targeting never gets that far, so the rollout result does not matter.

- "out_of_rollout" would need targeting to pass first.
- "disabled" is reserved for `!flag.enabled`; this flag is enabled.
- "rollout" is the reason for a user inside the rollout who gets a weighted variant.

excerpts.quote: return { flagKey: flag.key, variant: control, reason: "not_targeted" };

items.title: Working out a sampled estimate by hand
items.body:
`estimateFromSample(400, 0.1)`: the estimate is round(400 / 0.1) = 4000, the observed count scaled up by the sample rate. The standard error is sqrt(400 * 0.9) / 0.1 = sqrt(360) / 0.1, about 189.7, and the 95% interval is 1.96 times that, about 372. `formatEstimate` shows that band relative to the estimate, 372 / 4000, about 9%.

- "~400 ±5%" forgets to scale the observed count up by the sample rate.
- "~4,000 exactly" misreads the reliability floor: 30 observed events only decides `reliable`; a sampled number is never shown without its ±.
- "~40,000 ±1%" divides by the square of the rate, which the code never does.

excerpts.quote: const se = Math.sqrt(observed * (1 - sampleRate)) / sampleRate;
**Never render a sampled number as exact.**

items.title: The earliest step-1 event is the only anchor
items.body:
The anchor is written in one place, inside `if (level === 0)`. After the day-0 view, `level` is 1, so the day-6 view matches nothing the walker is looking for (it wants step 2) and is skipped. The signup on day 8 is compared with anchor 0: 8 > 7, rejected. The person stays at step 1.

- "The day-6 view re-anchors" describes a different funnel design (latest anchor); rule 1 says the earliest step-1 event anchors everything.
- "Any step-1 event within 7 days of the signup" is not a rule anywhere in the code.
- "A repeated step-1 event disqualifies the person" is wrong: they still count at step 1.

excerpts.quote: A person "enters" the funnel at their **earliest** step-1 event within the lookback

items.title: Ramping a rollout never moves existing users
items.body:
The rollout gate is `bucket(flag.key, ctx.distinctId, "rollout") >= flag.rolloutPercentage / 100`. The draw depends on the key, the salt and the user, not on the percentage. A user whose draw was below 0.10 is also below 0.20, so they stay in; the ramp only admits users with draws between 0.10 and 0.20.

- "Reshuffled" would need the draw to change; nothing in its input changed.
- "Removed until a new assignment table" is wrong: there is no assignment table at all.
- "A new variant" is wrong too: the variant pick uses its own "variant" salt and the same inputs, so it is also unchanged.

To re-randomize on purpose you change the flag key, which starts a new experiment.

excerpts.quote: if (rolloutDraw >= flag.rolloutPercentage / 100) {
it never moves someone who was already in.

items.title: The 60-second "undead key" window
items.body:
Authenticating every `POST /e` with a database lookup would make auth the bottleneck, so the resolver caches the hash-to-key mapping in process. Each cache entry expires `ttlMs` after it was stored, and `ttlMs` defaults to 60_000. A key revoked in the database keeps working on that instance until its cached entry expires: at most 60 seconds. ADR-0003 states this cost on purpose.

- "Not at all" describes an instant cache-bust on revoke, which does not exist yet: the ADR only says the management side "can add an instant cache-bust later".
- "For the process lifetime" is wrong: entries have an expiry time.
- "24 hours" mixes in `lastUsedAt`, which is a ~1% sampled write and has nothing to do with expiry.

excerpts.quote: this.ttlMs = opts.ttlMs ?? 60_000;
**a revoked key keeps working for up to 60s** ("undead key")
management side can add an instant cache-bust later

items.title: The window is measured from step 1, not the previous step
items.body:
The view on day 0 sets `anchor` (funnel.ts:58). The signup on day 5 passes `t <= anchor + windowMs` (5 <= 7) and the level becomes 2. The purchase on day 9 is checked against the SAME anchor: 9 > 0 + 7, so it is rejected. The person counts at steps 1 and 2.

- "Within 7 days of the signup" is the rule Pulse deliberately did not choose; the doc calls the choice a product decision with revenue implications.
- "Only bounds the gap between neighbours" is the same mistake in other words.
- "The signup resets the anchor" is wrong: the anchor is only assigned while `level === 0`.

excerpts.quote: } else if (level < n && matchesStep(e, spec.steps[level]) && t <= anchor + windowMs) {
The window is measured from step 1**, not from the previous step.

items.title: Why the window edge is inside the window
items.body:
The check at funnel.ts:62 is `t <= anchor + windowMs`, with `<=`, not `<`, and it is the same check for every step after the first. A step at exactly anchor + 7 days therefore counts; one millisecond later fails. The contract states it the same way, so analysts and the code agree.

- "Half-open, ending just before" would need `<`.
- "Only for the last step, with a strict < for earlier steps" is wrong: there is a single comparison, and line 62 applies `<=` to every step after the first.
- "Rounded to whole days" is wrong: `windowMs` is `spec.windowDays * DAY_MS` and timestamps are compared in milliseconds.

excerpts.quote: const windowMs = spec.windowDays * DAY_MS;
A conversion at *exactly* anchor + window counts; one millisecond later
